title: About
text: This is a blog about Jaddle, a project I’m working on.

title: A Gentle Tour of Saddle Point Solvers
text: Many of the hardest problems in machine learning and engineering are optimisation problems. Sometimes there’s a catch: you want the cheapest design, but it must satisfy certain rules. Saddle point solvers are one of the most elegant ways to handle that catch, and the path to understanding them is a story about turning rules into a game.

title: A Gentle Tour of Saddle Point Solvers
section: Step 1: Turn the rules into a fight
text:
Step 1: Turn the rules into a fight
Suppose you want to minimise a cost, but you must obey a rule. A classic trick is to add a penalty for breaking the rule and let a second player decide how big that penalty should be.
Call the first player X, who is trying to make the cost as small as possible. Call the second player Y, who is trying to make the penalty as large as possible whenever the rule is broken. Y is a bit of a troublemaker. If X breaks a rule, Y pounces and charges X for it.
Mathematicians call this dualising the constraints. A problem that said, “minimise the cost, subject to the rules” becomes “X minimises, while Y maximises, a combined score.” The problem has gone from a minimisation to a min-max.

title: A Gentle Tour of Saddle Point Solvers
text:
Step 2: Meet the two-player game
What we’ve built is a two-player zero-sum game. One player’s gain is exactly the other’s loss. X wants the score low, Y wants it high, and neither can simply walk away.
Picture a tug-of-war on a seesaw. Every move X makes pushes the score up or down, and every move Y makes pushes it back. Neither player is trying to be nice.

title: A Gentle Tour of Saddle Point Solvers
section: Step 3: The sweet spot is a Nash equilibrium
text:
Step 3: The sweet spot is a Nash equilibrium
In game theory, a Nash equilibrium is a situation where neither player can improve their outcome by changing their move alone. Each player is doing the best they can, given what the other is doing.
In our min-max game, this equilibrium has a lovely geometric name: a saddle point. Think of a horse’s saddle. Walk along it from front to back and you’re climbing up; walk side to side and you’re going down. The saddle point is the spot that is the lowest in one direction and the highest in the other at the same time.
That is exactly the answer to our original problem. The saddle point gives us the best design that also obeys the rules.

title: A Gentle Tour of Saddle Point Solvers
section: Step 4: Let the players learn from each other
text:
Step 4: Let the players learn from each other
How do we actually find the saddle point? One approach is to let both players learn as they play. Each player watches what the other has been doing and adjusts their strategy accordingly.
The simplest version is called gradient descent-ascent. X takes a small step downhill on the score, Y takes a small step uphill, and both repeat. It is like two hikers feeling their way across a foggy landscape, one trying to get lower and the other trying to get higher, each reacting to where the other has just stepped.

title: A Gentle Tour of Saddle Point Solvers
text:
Step 5: The twist (and the magic)
Here is the honest bit. In general, these learning dynamics don’t converge. In some games, the players chase each other in circles, or their steps grow larger and the game spirals away from the answer. Two stubborn players reacting instantly to each other are a recipe for wobbling.
But then something rather magical happens. If you stop looking at each individual move and instead track the long-running average of what each player has done, the averages settle down. The wobbles cancel out, and the averaged strategies drift steadily towards the saddle point, the Nash equilibrium, the answer we were looking for.

title: A Gentle Tour of Saddle Point Solvers
text:
Why it matters
Saddle point problems appear everywhere: training generative adversarial networks, robust control under uncertainty, fair resource allocation, and constrained learning in general. The core lesson is delightfully simple. When two opposing learners keep playing, don’t trust any single moment. Trust the average over time.

title: A Gentle Tour of Saddle Point Solvers
text:
From Idea to Engine: Jaddle
Everything above is a story about ideas: turn the rules into a fight, find the calm point where neither player wants to move, let both learners adapt, and trust the long-run average. Turning those ideas into code that actually runs fast is what Jaddle is for.
Jaddle (short for JAX Saddle Point Solver) is a library built on JAX, Google’s numerical computing library. It takes the two-player picture seriously. You describe the game, one player minimising and one maximising, and Jaddle runs the learning dynamics for you.
Here’s how the story maps onto the library:

Dualising the constraints becomes a function you write: the cost, plus the penalised constraints, as one combined score.
The two-player game is the object Jaddle solves. Each player’s update is computed from the gradient of that shared score, so you never hand-derive the learning rules.
The Nash equilibrium is the output you care about: the saddle point, the pair of strategies where neither player gains by moving alone.
Learning from the other player is the iterative update loop, with both players stepping at once and reacting to each other.
The long-running average is where the magic from the last section lives in practice.

JAX makes this practical. Automatic differentiation supplies the gradients, jit compiles the update step so it runs at speed, and vmap lets many problems run side by side. The same code runs on CPU, GPU, or TPU without rewriting.
So if the earlier sections gave you the intuition, Jaddle is the workshop where you put it to use. Try it on a small game first, watch the iterates wobble, then watch the averages settle. That moment is worth seeing for yourself.

title: How Jaddle Works
text:
WarningWarning: nerd content ahead!



This article is a bit nerdy. There are equations, Greek letters and at least one joke about horse saddles. You don’t need to understand every symbol: the words around each equation say what it means in plain language. If an equation looks scary, read the sentence after it and keep going.
You have been warned. Be prepared!

title: How Jaddle Works
text:
What problem are we solving?
Jaddle is a program that solves optimisation problems. That means: pick some numbers so that something is as small (or as big) as possible, while following a set of rules.
Here is a tiny one. You are baking. Flour costs $2 a kilo, and your recipe needs at least 3 kilos. How much flour should you buy to spend as little as possible?
You already know the answer: buy exactly 3 kilos and spend $6. Easy.
Now imagine an airline planning thousands of flights, a power company deciding which power stations to switch on, or a delivery company routing hundreds of trucks. These problems have millions of numbers to choose and millions of rules to follow. Nobody can eyeball those. We need a recipe that a computer can follow, step by step, and that recipe is what this article is about.
Mathematicians write this kind of problem (a linear program) like this:
\[
\text{minimise } c^\top x \quad \text{such that} \quad Ax \le b, \quad \ell \le x \le u
\]
In words:

\(x\) is the list of numbers we get to choose (how much of each thing to buy).
\(c\) is the list of prices, and \(c^\top x = c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2 + \dots\) is the total cost.
Each row of \(Ax \le b\) is one rule (“you need at least this much of that”).
\(\ell \le x \le u\) are simple limits on each number, like “you can’t buy a negative amount of flour”.

For the flour problem there is just one number, \(x\) = kilos of flour. The cost is \(2x\), the rule is \(x \ge 3\) (which we can write as \(3 - x \le 0\)) and the limit is \(x \ge 0\).
Jaddle solves these problems in five big ideas. Let’s go through them one at a time.

title: How Jaddle Works
section: 1. Turn rules into fines (dualising and the Lagrangian)
text:
1. Turn rules into fines (dualising and the Lagrangian)
Rules are awkward for computers. They act like invisible walls, and walls are hard to deal with when there are millions of them.
So we play a trick: we replace every rule with a fine.
Imagine a referee who watches the shopper. For each rule, the referee chooses a fine, \(y\), to charge for every kilo you are short. If you buy \(x\) kilos you are \(3 - x\) kilos short, so the fine is \(y \times (3 - x)\). Your total bill becomes
\[
L(x, y) = \underbrace{2x}_{\text{cost of flour}} + \underbrace{y\,(3 - x)}_{\text{fine for being short}}
\]
This bill has a famous name: the Lagrangian, after Joseph-Louis Lagrange, a mathematician from the 1700s. For any linear program it looks like this:
\[
L(x, y) = c^\top x + y^\top (A x - b), \qquad y \ge 0
\]
There is one fine for each rule, and the list of fines \(y\) is called the dual variables. (The shopper’s numbers \(x\) are the primal variables.) Swapping rules for fines like this is called dualising the constraints. Fines can’t be negative, because a referee doesn’t pay you for breaking a rule. If you have extra flour, \(3 - x\) is negative, and the referee’s best move is to set the fine to zero. (Rules of the form “exactly equal to” also work. Their fines are allowed to be negative.)

A game with two players
Now we have a game:

The shopper chooses \(x\) and wants the bill \(L\) to be as small as possible.
The referee chooses \(y\) and wants the bill \(L\) to be as big as possible.

\[
\min_{x} \; \max_{y \ge 0} \; L(x, y)
\]
Why does this game give the same answer as the original problem? If the shopper breaks the rule, the referee can make the fine enormous, so breaking the rule is a terrible idea. If the shopper follows the rule, the fine does nothing. The shopper’s best move is to follow the rules and spend as little as possible, which is exactly the original problem. The difference is that there are no walls any more, just a bill to push down and fines to push up.


The saddle point
For the flour problem the game ends at \(x = 3\) and \(y = 2\). Check it:

If the referee sets \(y = 2\), the bill is \(2x + 2(3 - x) = 6\) whatever \(x\) is. The shopper can’t do any better by changing \(x\).
If the shopper buys \(x = 3\), the bill is \(6 + y \times 0 = 6\) whatever \(y\) is. The referee can’t do any better by changing \(y\).

Neither player wants to move. This spot is called a saddle point, because the bill looks like a horse saddle. Along the horse’s back the saddle curves up on both sides, so the middle is the lowest point (what the shopper wants). Across the horse it curves down on both sides, so the middle is the highest point (what the referee wants). The middle of a saddle is the lowest point one way and the highest point the other way.
That is where the name comes from: Jaddle = JAX + saddle.






TipBonus: fines are prices



The answer \(y = 2\) means something. If your recipe needed one more kilo, your cost would go up by exactly $2. The referee’s fine tells you how much each rule costs you. On big problems this is very useful: it tells a company which of its rules are the expensive ones.

title: How Jaddle Works
section: 2. Take turns walking downhill and uphill (alternating gradient descent–ascent)

title: How Jaddle Works
section: 3. The average is smarter than the walker (averaging)
text:
3. The average is smarter than the walker (averaging)
What is in the middle of a circle? The centre! And if you take lots of points spread evenly around a circle and average them, you land near the centre.
So Jaddle keeps a running average of everywhere the players have been. Write \(z = (x, y)\) for both players’ positions together. After \(N\) turns the average is
\[
\bar z_N = \frac{\eta_1 z_1 + \eta_2 z_2 + \dots + \eta_N z_N}{\eta_1 + \eta_2 + \dots + \eta_N}
\]
Each position is weighted by the step size \(\eta_n\) used to reach it (more on \(\eta\) in the next section), so bigger steps count for more. Jaddle doesn’t store every old position. It nudges the average a little towards each new point, which costs almost nothing.
Think of a dog on a lead running in circles around a post. Take a photo every second and average the dog’s position over all the photos: you get the post.
The orange line below is the average. Turn up the number of turns and watch it home in on the answer.

viewof eta2 = Inputs.range([0.05, 1.2], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Step size"})
viewof n2 = Inputs.range([5, 300], {value: 150, step: 5, label: "Number of turns"})
saddlePlot(simulate(eta2, n2), true)






















There is a catch. The average gets there slowly: to be 10 times more accurate you need about 10 times more turns. It also never forgets. The very first guesses, which were far from the answer, keep dragging the average away forever. We fix both problems in section 5.

title: How Jaddle Works
text:
4. Choosing step sizes: \(\eta\), \(k\), \(t\) and \(s\)
Steps that are too big overshoot and fly off. Steps that are too small take forever. Worse, different numbers in the same problem can need very different step sizes. One might be measured in millimetres and another in kilometres.
Jaddle builds every step size out of four pieces:
\[
\tau_j = \frac{\eta}{k}\, t_j \qquad\qquad \sigma_i = \eta\, k\, s_i
\]
\(\tau_j\) is the step for the shopper’s \(j\)-th number, and \(\sigma_i\) is the step for the referee’s \(i\)-th fine. Think of a group out on a hike:

Before any of this starts, Jaddle rescales the problem so that the numbers in \(A\), \(b\) and \(c\) are all roughly the same size. It is a bit like converting every measurement to the same units. (The methods are called Ruiz and Pock–Chambolle scaling, if you want to look them up.) On top of that, \(t\) and \(s\) start at 1 and are then adapted as the solver learns more about the problem. Giving each number its own multiplier like this is called diagonal preconditioning: “diagonal” because if you wrote the multipliers into a table, they would only appear along its diagonal.

\(\eta\): a step that checks itself
Nobody tells Jaddle the right step size. It works it out as it goes, like this.
Take a trial step. Then measure two things:
\[
\text{movement} = k\,\lVert \Delta x\rVert^2 + \frac{1}{k}\,\lVert \Delta y \rVert^2
\qquad\qquad
\text{interaction} = \big|\,\Delta y^\top A\, \Delta x\,\big|
\]
\(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) are how much each player changed, and \(\lVert \Delta x \rVert^2\) means “square each change and add them up”. The movement is how far the players went. The interaction is how hard their two moves pushed against each other through the rules in \(A\).
The interaction is what causes trouble. When the shopper’s move and the referee’s move push on each other too hard, they overreact and fly off. When the moves are big compared with how much they disturb each other, the step is safe. The largest safe step is
\[
\bar\eta = \frac{\text{movement}}{2 \times \text{interaction}}
\]

If \(\eta\) was bigger than \(\bar\eta\), the step was too greedy. Jaddle throws it away, shrinks \(\eta\) to just under \(\bar\eta\), and tries again.
If \(\eta\) was safe, Jaddle keeps the step and lets \(\eta\) grow a little for next time:

\[
\eta_{\text{next}} = \min\Big(\; \big(1 - (n+1)^{-0.3}\big)\,\bar\eta, \;\;\; \big(1 + (n+1)^{-0.6}\big)\,\eta \;\Big)
\]
Don’t worry about the odd powers; \(n\) just counts the steps taken so far. The first part says “stay a bit below the safe limit”. The second says “grow, but by less and less as time goes on”. At the start \(\eta\) can grow by up to 66% in one go. After a thousand steps it can only grow by about 1.6%.
This means Jaddle never needs to know in advance how big \(A\) can make things, which is expensive to work out for a huge problem. It also fixes a bad starting guess for \(\eta\) within a few steps. (When \(t\) and \(s\) are switched on, the movement is measured with each number’s change divided by its own \(t_j\) or \(s_i\), but the idea is the same.)


\(k\): who should walk faster?
Sometimes the shopper is nearly at the answer while the referee still has a long way to go, or the other way round. \(k\) shares the step between them: a bigger \(k\) makes the referee’s steps longer (\(\eta k\)) and the shopper’s shorter (\(\eta / k\)). It doesn’t make the steps riskier overall, because the two step sizes multiplied together are always \(\eta^2\), whatever \(k\) is.
Jaddle updates \(k\) at every restart (section 5). It looks at how far each player travelled during the last stretch:
\[
k_{\text{target}} = \frac{\lVert \Delta y \rVert}{\lVert \Delta x \rVert}
\]
If the referee travelled further, the referee probably still has further to go, so the referee should get the longer stride. Jaddle doesn’t jump straight to the target, because one stretch of measurements can be misleading. It meets the old value halfway, in the multiplying sense:
\[
k_{\text{new}} = \sqrt{k_{\text{old}} \times k_{\text{target}}}
\]
This is the geometric mean. For example, if \(k_{\text{old}} = 1\) and \(k_{\text{target}} = 100\), then \(k_{\text{new}} = \sqrt{100} = 10\). Why not the ordinary average? Because \(k\) is a ratio. \(k = 100\) and \(k = 1/100\) are equally lopsided, just in opposite directions, and the geometric mean treats them fairly. Jaddle also keeps \(k\) between \(10^{-8}\) and \(10^{8}\) so it can never run away. The very first \(k\) is a guess based on the sizes of \(c\) and \(b\).


\(t\) and \(s\): every number gets its own stride
\(\eta\) and \(k\) treat big groups of numbers the same. But inside a problem with a million numbers, some are marching steadily towards their answer while others are jittering back and forth. \(t\) and \(s\) give each number its own stride.
At each restart, Jaddle looks back over the last stretch at each number \(j\) and works out two things:

its net distance \(r_j\): how far it ended up from where it started;
its total wiggle \(H_j\): the size of every step it took, squared and added up.

Then it divides one by the other:
\[
\rho_j = \frac{r_j}{\sqrt{H_j}}
\]
Here is what \(\rho\) (rho) looks like for three numbers that each took 16 steps of size 1, so \(\sqrt{H} = \sqrt{16} = 4\) for all of them:

A big \(\rho\) means the number knows where it is going, so it should take bigger steps. A small \(\rho\) means it keeps overshooting and coming back, so it should take smaller steps. Jaddle updates each number’s stride with
\[
t_j \;\leftarrow\; t_j \times \left(\frac{\rho_j}{\rho_{\text{typical}}}\right)^{1/2}
\]
where \(\rho_{\text{typical}}\) is the geometric mean of all the \(\rho\)’s. If only A and B were in the problem, \(\rho_{\text{typical}} = \sqrt{4 \times 1} = 2\):

A’s stride is multiplied by \(\sqrt{4/2} \approx 1.41\), so it gets 41% longer.
B’s stride is multiplied by \(\sqrt{1/2} \approx 0.71\), so it gets 29% shorter.

Dividing by the typical value keeps the group’s overall pace the same, so \(\eta\) and \(k\) stay in charge of that. Each stride is also kept within 10 times bigger or smaller than where it started, and numbers that didn’t move at all (for example ones stuck at a limit) give no information, so they keep their stride. The referee’s fines get exactly the same treatment to update \(s_i\).
This idea borrows from machine learning methods called AdaGrad and DoG (“distance over gradients”). On a standard collection of hard test problems (the MIPLIB 2017 linear programs) it cut Jaddle’s solve times by about 18% on average.

title: How Jaddle Works
section: 5. Restarts: when in doubt, start fresh

title: How Jaddle Works
text:
Putting it all together
Here is the whole recipe in one place:
rescale the problem so its numbers are all about the same size
start with x = 0 (inside its limits), y = 0, η = 1, k = a guess, all t and s = 1

repeat:
    take a trial alternating step with τ = (η / k)·t and σ = η·k·s
    if the step was too big:  shrink η and try again
    otherwise:                keep it, update the average, let η grow a little

    every so often:
        work out the wrongness score
        if all three checks are tiny:  stop, we have the answer!
        if a restart rule fires:
            jump to the better of the current point and the average
            update k, t and s
            start a fresh average
Every part of this is either a multiplication by \(A\) or \(A^\top\), or simple arithmetic on each number separately. There are no big equation-solving steps, which is why it works on problems with millions of numbers and runs so well on graphics cards. Jaddle is written in JAX, a Python library that turns the whole loop into one fast compiled program. The same code runs on a laptop CPU, a GPU or a TPU.
Jaddle also has a second solver for curvier problems (convex programs), where the cost and rules can be more complicated than straight lines. It uses the same five ideas. The only difference is that it can’t write the slopes down as \(c + A^\top y\), so JAX works them out automatically.

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
text:
Imagine a bank that wants to save time. Instead of a person reading every loan application, it wants a computer program to read them and say “yes” or “no”. To teach the program, the bank hands over a big pile of old decisions made by its human loan officers and says: learn to do what they did.
That sounds sensible. But there is a catch. What if the old decisions were unfair?

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
section: A world with a thumb on the scale
text:
A world with a thumb on the scale
In this example we build a small make-believe world so we can see exactly what is going on. There are applicants from two groups, which we’ll call Group A and Group B. About three in ten applicants belong to Group B.
Every applicant has a few “skill” scores, things like income stability or repayment history. Here is the important part: the skills are spread out in exactly the same way in both groups. Nobody in Group B is any less capable, on average, than anyone in Group A.
In a fair world, whether you get a loan depends only on those skills. But the historical decisions the bank kept came from a world with a thumb on the scale. Every Group B applicant had a fixed amount knocked off their chances, just for being in Group B.
So the pile of old decisions, the one we’re asking the computer to learn from, quietly contains a bias.

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
text:
“Just don’t tell it the group!”
The first idea most people have is simple: don’t show the computer which group each applicant is in. If it can’t see the group, surely it can’t discriminate?
Sadly, it isn’t that easy. In our world, each applicant also has two extra details, a bit like a postcode, that happen to differ a little between the groups. They say nothing about whether someone will repay a loan. They are what statisticians call proxies: clues that let you guess the group without being told.
A computer trained to copy the old decisions is very good at spotting patterns. It notices that applicants with a certain kind of “postcode” were turned down more often, and it learns to lean on that clue. Sure enough, when we train a plain model, it puts a negative weight on those postcode-like features and approves Group B applicants far less often than Group A.






NoteThe lesson



Hiding a sensitive attribute is not the same as being fair. If other information can stand in for it, a model can rebuild the bias on its own.

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
text:
How the robot banker thinks
The model we use is called logistic regression, and it is one of the oldest and most trusted tools in machine learning. You can think of it as a points system:

Each feature (each skill score, each postcode detail) earns or loses the applicant some points.
The points are added up into a single score.
If the score is above zero, the answer is “yes”. Below zero, “no”.

“Learning” just means adjusting how many points each feature is worth until the model’s answers match the training data as closely as possible. Finding the best point values is an optimisation problem: a search for the settings that make some measure of error as small as it can be.

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
text:
Adding a fairness rule
To push back against the bias, we give the optimiser an extra rule to obey while it learns. The rule we want is demographic parity: both groups should be approved at the same rate.
There is a small snag. Approval rates jump in steps: one applicant flips from “no” to “yes” and the rate suddenly hops. Optimisers prefer smooth hills to staircases. So, following a well-known approach by Zafar and colleagues (2017), we use a smoother stand-in for the rule:

The model’s average score shouldn’t depend on which group you’re in.

We also add a dial, which we’ll call the fairness bound. Turn the dial all the way up and there’s no rule at all: you get the plain, biased model. Turn it all the way down to zero and the two groups must have exactly the same average score. Anywhere in between is a compromise.

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
text:
What we found
We trained two models: one with no fairness rule, and one with the dial at zero.
The fair model closes most of the gap in approval rates between the two groups. And something interesting happens to its accuracy:

Measured against the biased historical decisions, the fair model looks worse. Of course it does: it is refusing to copy the bias.
Measured against the fair decisions (the ones that depend only on skill), the fair model looks better.

In real life we would never get to see those “fair decisions”. We only know them here because we built the world ourselves. But it shows something important: if the bias lives in the labels rather than in the people, then “accuracy against the past” can be a misleading report card.

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
section: The whole trade-off in one go
text:
The whole trade-off in one go
One fair model and one unfair model only tell part of the story. What about all the settings in between?
We picked 40 different positions for the fairness dial and asked Jaddle, the optimisation library this example is built with, to train all 40 models at the same time, as one batch. That gives us a full curve showing how accuracy changes as the model becomes fairer, rather than a couple of dots.
Reading the curve from the unfair end to the fair end, accuracy against the biased labels slides down while accuracy against the fair labels climbs up.

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
text:
The price of fairness
Here is my favourite part. When an optimiser obeys a rule, it can also tell you how much that rule is costing. Mathematicians call this a dual variable or shadow price. Think of it as a receipt that comes with each answer, saying: “if you tightened this rule by one more notch, the training error would go up by this much.”
For our fairness rule, that receipt is a price of fairness. We found that:

When the dial is loose enough that the rule isn’t actually stopping anything, the price is zero. The rule is just along for the ride.
As the dial tightens, the price climbs steadily. Each extra step towards equal treatment costs a little more than the one before.

That’s useful information for real decision-makers. Rather than arguing in the abstract about whether fairness is “worth it”, you can see the actual exchange rate and talk about it openly.

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
text:
A few footnotes
Fairness is a deep and much-debated subject, and this example is a small, tidy illustration rather than a final answer.

Demographic parity is only one definition of fairness. Others ask for equal error rates, or equal treatment of similar individuals. They can disagree with each other, and choosing between them is a question about values, not just maths.
Our world is made up. Real data is messier, and real bias is rarely a single fixed penalty.
The rule we used is a stand-in. Making average scores equal tends to bring approval rates together, but it doesn’t guarantee they match exactly.

title: Teaching a Robot Banker to Play Fair
text:
The takeaway
A model trained to imitate the past will happily imitate the past’s mistakes, even when you hide the obvious clues. Adding a fairness rule to the optimisation is a direct, transparent way to push back. And because the optimiser hands you a price for every rule it follows, you can see exactly what that fairness is costing, and decide with your eyes open.

title: Ignoring the Fibbers
text:
Imagine you’re trying to follow a remote-controlled boat drifting around a pond, but you can’t see it directly. Instead, a friend on the bank shouts out its position every few seconds. Most of the time they’re pretty accurate, give or take a little. But your friend is easily distracted, and about one time in five they shout out something completely off, as if they’d glanced at a duck instead.
Can you still work out where the boat actually went?

title: Ignoring the Fibbers
text:
Two sources of information
You have two things to go on:

The measurements, your friend’s shouted positions. Most are close; some are wild.
The physics. Boats don’t teleport. They glide along, speeding up and slowing down smoothly, nudged now and then by gusts of wind you can’t predict.

The trick is to combine them. You’re looking for a path that obeys the physics and stays reasonably close to the measurements. If a measurement says the boat jumped five metres to the left in an instant, the physics says “that’s not possible”, and the path should mostly ignore it.
Finding the best such path, after the fact, using all the measurements at once, is called smoothing.

title: Ignoring the Fibbers
section: The classic recipe: the Kalman smoother
text:
The classic recipe: the Kalman smoother
In the 1960s, Rudolf Kalman developed a beautifully efficient method for exactly this kind of problem. Versions of his ideas helped steer the Apollo spacecraft to the Moon, and today they run inside phones, cars, drones and countless other gadgets.
The classic approach chooses the path that keeps two things small at once:

the wind gusts needed to explain the path (smaller gusts mean a more natural path), and
the misses, the gaps between the path and each measurement.

To combine all the misses into one number, it squares each one and adds them up. Squaring makes sense when errors are small and well-behaved: it treats misses in either direction equally and is very convenient mathematically.

title: Ignoring the Fibbers
text:
The problem with squaring
Squaring has a weakness. A miss that’s twice as big counts four times as much. A miss that’s twenty times as big counts four hundred times as much.
In our example, the occasional wild measurement is about twenty times noisier than a normal one. So when the classic smoother tries to keep the squared misses small, those few wild measurements dominate everything. They act like bullies, dragging the estimated path towards themselves, because ignoring them would be “too expensive”.
It’s a bit like a teacher averaging test scores where one student’s answer of “a million” for a question with answer “seven” drags the class average into the stratosphere.

title: Ignoring the Fibbers
section: A fairer referee: the Huber penalty
text:
A fairer referee: the Huber penalty
The fix is to change how misses are scored. Instead of squaring every miss, we use the Huber penalty, named after the statistician Peter Huber:

For small misses, it behaves just like squaring. Normal, everyday noise is treated exactly as before.
For big misses, it switches to growing in a straight line. A miss twice as big costs only about twice as much, not four times.







TipA helpful way to picture it



The squared penalty is like a rubber band that pulls harder and harder the further you stretch it. The Huber penalty is a rubber band that, beyond a certain point, stops getting stronger and just pulls with a steady force. Wild measurements still tug on the path, but they can no longer yank it off course.


This version is called the robust Kalman smoother. “Robust”, in statistics, means “doesn’t fall apart when some of the data is bad”.

title: Ignoring the Fibbers
text:
The experiment
We simulate an object moving around a flat plane for 50 seconds, measured 1,000 times. It has a position and a speed, a little friction slowing it down, and random pushes knocking it around. Each measurement has a one-in-five chance of being an outlier.
Then we estimate the path twice: once with the classic smoother and once with the robust one.
The results are striking. The classic smoother’s path is visibly dragged around by the outliers, wandering off towards the wild measurements. The robust smoother’s path sticks closely to the true trajectory, as if it had simply noticed which shouts to take with a pinch of salt.

title: Ignoring the Fibbers
text:
What Jaddle does differently
Both versions of the problem are written in CVXPY, a popular language for describing optimisation problems. In fact, this is one of CVXPY’s own showcase examples.
The classic smoother is a relatively simple kind of problem (a quadratic program), and Jaddle solves it directly.
The robust version is more interesting. Normally CVXPY would translate the Huber penalty into a bundle of cone-shaped rules, which works but makes the problem bigger and more complicated. Jaddle takes a different route: it keeps the Huber penalty as the smooth, gently curving function it really is, and solves the problem in that form. It also notices that the “miss” for each measurement is completely determined by the path, so it can drop those as separate unknowns and work with the path alone. Fewer moving parts, same answer.
We check both of Jaddle’s answers against Clarabel, a well-established solver that comes with CVXPY, and they agree.

title: Ignoring the Fibbers
text:
The takeaway
Real-world data is rarely perfectly behaved. Sensors glitch, signals bounce, people mishear. A method that assumes every measurement is roughly right can be thrown badly off course by a handful that aren’t.
By changing one small thing, how we score big misses, the robust Kalman smoother learns to listen to the crowd without being bullied by the loudest fibbers. It’s a good lesson beyond boats and ponds: when you’re combining lots of evidence, make sure no single piece gets to shout over all the rest.

title: How Much Wobble Can You Handle?
text:
Suppose someone hands you a pile of money and a list of 500 things you could invest it in. Some are expected to grow a lot. Some are expected to grow a little. All of them wobble up and down unpredictably. How do you decide what to buy?
If you only cared about growth, the answer would be easy: put everything into whatever is expected to grow fastest. But that’s like crossing a river by jumping onto the single biggest stepping stone: thrilling, until it wobbles. Most people would rather give up a little expected growth to sleep better at night.
This example explores that trade-off.

title: How Much Wobble Can You Handle?
text:
The rules of the game
We need to decide what fraction of our money goes into each of the 500 assets. The rules are:

The fractions must add up to 100%. We invest all the money, no more and no less.
No fraction can be negative. In finance-speak, the portfolio is long-only: we can’t bet against an asset or borrow to invest.
The portfolio’s volatility (how much it’s expected to wobble) must stay below a limit we choose.

Within those rules, we want the highest expected return.

title: How Much Wobble Can You Handle?
text:
Two kinds of wobble
To measure wobble, we use what’s called a factor model. It says each asset’s ups and downs come from two sources.
Shared wobble. Some forces push lots of assets around at once. Think of an ice-cream shop and a sunscreen company: a heatwave is good for both, and a rainy summer is bad for both. In our example there are 50 of these shared forces, or factors, and each asset reacts to them in its own way.
Personal wobble. Every asset also has its own private surprises. A particular shop might get a rave review or a broken freezer. These are unrelated to everything else.
This distinction matters because the two kinds of wobble behave differently when you combine assets:

Personal wobbles tend to cancel out. If you own lots of different things, one asset’s bad day is often balanced by another’s good day. This is the magic of diversification.
Shared wobbles don’t cancel. If all your assets love sunny weather, owning more of them doesn’t protect you from rain.

title: How Much Wobble Can You Handle?
section: Where the ice-cream cone comes in
text:
Where the ice-cream cone comes in
To work out a portfolio’s total wobble, you collect all its exposures, to each shared factor and to each asset’s personal risk, and measure their combined size, the way you’d measure the length of an arrow from its parts.
The rule “this combined size must be below the limit” has a surprising shape. If you drew all the portfolios that satisfy it (and let the limit itself vary), you’d get a shape like a cone. It even has a nickname among optimisation folk: the ice-cream cone. Its formal name is the second-order cone.
Why does that matter? Because some optimisation solvers can only handle flat-sided shapes, built from straight-line rules like “this plus that must be at most ten”. A cone has a curved, rounded surface, so those solvers can’t take it directly. Jaddle can: at each step it takes a stride towards a better answer, then gently pushes the result back inside the cone if it’s wandered out.

title: How Much Wobble Can You Handle?
text:
Tracing the efficient frontier
Rather than picking one wobble limit, we try five, ranging from cautious (6% volatility) to adventurous (20%). For each one, we find the best possible portfolio.
If you plot the results, with risk along the bottom and expected return up the side, you get a curve that finance people call the efficient frontier. Every point on it is a portfolio where you can’t get more expected return without accepting more risk. Any portfolio below the curve is leaving money on the table.
Two things make tracing this curve quicker:

Warm starts. Each new solve begins from the previous answer instead of from scratch. Moving the limit from 6% to 8% doesn’t change the best portfolio completely, so starting nearby saves a lot of work.
Reusing the setup. The problem is described once, and only the wobble limit changes between solves.

title: How Much Wobble Can You Handle?
text:
The slope tells a story
Every time the solver obeys a rule, it can also report how much that rule is costing. For the wobble limit, this number answers the question: “If I allowed a little more wobble, how much extra return would I get?”
That’s precisely the slope of the efficient frontier at that point, and it shrinks as the limit grows. When you’re being very cautious, accepting a bit more risk buys you a healthy boost in return. When you’re already being adventurous, each extra bit of risk buys less and less. Like adding sugar to tea: the first spoonful makes a big difference; the fifth, not so much.

title: How Much Wobble Can You Handle?
text:
What the portfolios look like
At the cautious end, the best portfolio is spread across many assets, leaning hard on diversification to cancel out personal wobbles.
As the limit loosens, the portfolio concentrates on fewer assets with higher expected returns. Freed from the need to stay calm, it stops spreading its bets and starts backing its favourites.

title: How Much Wobble Can You Handle?
text:
Checking our work
To make sure Jaddle’s answers are right, we solve every problem a second time with Clarabel, a well-respected solver that ships with CVXPY. The returns agree to within a tiny fraction of a percent, and so do the portfolios themselves.

title: How Much Wobble Can You Handle?
text:
The takeaway
Investing well isn’t just about picking winners. It’s about understanding how your choices wobble together. By describing risk as the size of an arrow, and using a solver that’s comfortable with the curved, cone-shaped rules that come with it, we can find, for any level of nerve, the best portfolio for that amount of risk. And we get a bonus: a clear reading of exactly how much extra return each extra bit of courage would buy.

title: The Goldilocks Battery
text:
Picture a building with solar panels on the roof. At midday the sun is blazing and the panels are churning out electricity. In the evening, when everyone gets home and turns on the oven, the TV and the kettle, the sun has gone down and the power has to come from the grid, at the most expensive time of day.
The obvious fix is a battery: soak up cheap or free energy when it’s plentiful and use it later when it’s pricey. But batteries aren’t free. Buy one that’s too small and you miss out on savings. Buy one that’s too big and you’ve paid for capacity you never use.
So how big should it be? Like Goldilocks, we’re looking for the one that’s just right.

title: The Goldilocks Battery
text:
Two questions hiding inside one
It turns out “how big a battery should I buy?” contains a second question tucked inside it: “how would I actually use it?”
You can’t judge a battery without knowing how it would be run. A big battery used badly might save less than a small battery used cleverly. So, to size the battery, we need to know how to operate it well on every kind of day it might face.
That gives us two layers:

The operating problem (every day): given a battery of a certain size, when should it charge and when should it discharge to make the electricity bill as small as possible?
The sizing problem (once): given that we’ll always run the battery as well as we can, which size gives the lowest total cost, counting both the battery’s price and the bills?

title: The Goldilocks Battery
text:
One day at a time
We split each day into 24 hours. Each hour has:

an electricity price, which peaks in the morning and, even more, in the evening;
a demand, the amount of power the building needs, which follows a similar pattern;
some solar output, which peaks around lunchtime and depends on how cloudy the day is.

The battery has two numbers that describe its size, and it’s worth knowing the difference:

Energy capacity (in kilowatt-hours) is how much it can store. Think of it as the size of a water tank.
Power rating (in kilowatts) is how fast it can charge or discharge. Think of it as the width of the tap.

A huge tank with a tiny tap can’t empty fast enough to cover the evening rush. A wide tap on a tiny tank runs dry in minutes. You need a sensible match.
Planning one day’s battery use, given the prices, the demand, the sunshine and the battery’s size, is a classic linear program: a puzzle where you choose a bunch of numbers (how much to charge, discharge and buy each hour) to minimise a cost, while obeying straightforward rules like “you can’t store more than the tank holds” and “the lights must stay on”. The battery also has to end the day as full as it started, so it can’t cheat by borrowing from tomorrow.

title: The Goldilocks Battery
text:
Thirty-two days of weather
One day isn’t enough to make a decision. Some days are sunny, some are gloomy, and prices bounce around. So we generate 32 sample days, each with its own mix of prices, demand and sunshine, and judge each battery size by its average performance across all of them.
That means every time we want to test a battery size, we have to solve 32 operating puzzles. That could get slow.

title: The Goldilocks Battery
text:
The bulk-discount twist
There’s one more wrinkle, and it’s the reason this example exists. Batteries enjoy economies of scale: a bigger battery costs more, but not proportionally more. In our model, doubling the battery’s size makes it about 1.74 times as expensive, not twice as expensive.
That sounds like good news for your wallet, and it is. But it’s bad news for the maths. If cost were perfectly proportional to size, the whole thing (sizing plus all 32 days) could be bundled into one giant linear program and solved directly, very quickly. The bulk discount bends the cost curve, and that bend breaks the neat linear structure. We need a different approach.

title: The Goldilocks Battery
text:
Feeling for the slope
Here is the trick. Imagine you’re standing on a hillside in thick fog, and you want to reach the bottom of the valley. You can’t see the bottom, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a step downhill, feel again, take another step, and so on. This is called gradient descent, and it’s one of the most widely used ideas in all of computing.
To use it, we need the slope: if we made the battery a tiny bit bigger, would the total cost go up or down, and by how much?
The lovely part is that the operating puzzles hand us this information for free. When a linear program finishes, its solution comes with extra numbers that say how much the best possible cost would change if each limit were loosened a little. One of those limits is “the battery can’t hold more than its capacity”, so the solver already knows how much a slightly bigger battery would have saved on that day. We don’t have to do any extra work to get the slope.
Jaddle solves all 32 daily puzzles at once, in a single batch, collects the slopes, and combines them with the slope of the battery’s price. Then we take a step downhill and repeat. Forty steps later, we’ve arrived.

title: The Goldilocks Battery
text:
The answer
Across our 32 sample days:

With no battery, the site spends about $6.02 per day on electricity.
With the battery that gradient descent found, the total daily cost (battery and bills) drops to about $3.83 per day.

The best battery stores roughly 14 to 15 kilowatt-hours.

title: The Goldilocks Battery
section: Did we find the real bottom?
text:
Did we find the real bottom?
Because of that bulk-discount bend, the landscape isn’t a perfectly smooth bowl. Gradient descent always walks downhill, but it can get stuck in a small dip that isn’t the deepest point. And there’s no exact solver for this problem we can check against.
So we did the next best thing: we started again from a completely different place. The first run began with a tiny battery and grew it. The second began with an absurdly oversized battery and shrank it. Both hikers walked down through the fog and met in the same valley. Their costs agreed to within 0.03%.
Their battery sizes agreed slightly less closely (about 14.3 versus 14.6 kilowatt-hours). That’s not a problem; it tells us the valley floor is wide and flat. Near the best size, a little bigger or a little smaller makes almost no difference to the cost. That’s handy in real life, where batteries only come in certain sizes anyway.

title: The Goldilocks Battery
text:
What the battery actually does
If you look at the plan for the sunniest day, the battery behaves just as you’d hope. It fills up around midday when the solar panels are producing more than the building needs, then drains during the expensive evening peak, cutting the amount of power bought from the grid when prices are highest.

title: The Goldilocks Battery
text:
The takeaway
Big decisions often depend on lots of small ones. Here, a one-off purchase depends on thousands of hour-by-hour choices across many different days. By solving all the small problems together, and using the slopes they give away for free, we can steer the big decision step by step until it’s just right. Not too big, not too small.

title: Herding a Thousand Springy Robots
text:
Imagine four blocks sitting in a row on a slippery table, joined to each other by springs, with the two end blocks also attached by springs to walls. Give one a poke and the whole chain starts jiggling back and forth. Now add three little motors, one between each neighbouring pair of blocks, that can push them apart or pull them together. And just to make life interesting, every so often a random shove knocks the blocks around.
Your job is to keep the chain calm, and keep every block within a safe zone around its resting spot.
Now imagine doing that for a thousand chains at once.

title: Herding a Thousand Springy Robots
text:
The jiggling-blocks system
This setup comes from a well-known 2010 research paper by Yang Wang and Stephen Boyd, and it’s become a standard test for control methods. The rules are:

Each motor has a strength limit. It can only push or pull so hard.
Each block should stay within a safe zone around its resting position.
We want the blocks to settle down without the motors working harder than necessary.

title: Herding a Thousand Springy Robots
text:
Thinking ahead: model predictive control
How do you decide what the motors should do? One of the most powerful approaches is called model predictive control, or MPC.
MPC works a lot like a good chess player:

Look at the board. Measure where every block is and how fast it’s moving.
Think several moves ahead. Using a model of how springs and blocks behave, plan the best sequence of motor pushes for the next 15 steps (about seven and a half seconds).
Make only the first move. Apply the first push in the plan.
Look again and re-plan. The world never goes exactly as predicted (those random shoves!), so throw the old plan away and make a fresh one from the new position.

This loop of plan, act, re-plan makes MPC both clever and adaptable. It’s used in self-driving cars, chemical plants, robots, drones and even some heating systems.
Each plan is a small optimisation puzzle called a quadratic program, with 105 numbers to choose and 120 rules to obey.

title: Herding a Thousand Springy Robots
section: Soft walls instead of hard ones
text:
Soft walls instead of hard ones
There’s a subtle problem. Sometimes a random shove knocks a block so hard that no plan, however clever, can keep it inside its safe zone. If the rules said “the block must stay inside, no exceptions”, the puzzle would have no solution and the controller would be stuck.
So the safe zones are made soft. A block is allowed to stray outside, but the plan pays a hefty fine for every bit it goes over. The fine is large enough that whenever staying inside is possible, the plan does exactly that. It’s only when there’s no other choice that a block is allowed to go a little over, and even then the plan does its best to bring it back.
The motor limits, on the other hand, stay hard. A motor physically can’t push harder than its maximum, so the plan is never allowed to ask it to.

title: Herding a Thousand Springy Robots
section: One at a time versus all together
text:
One at a time versus all together
A single one of these puzzles is tiny. A good solver running on an ordinary computer processor (CPU) can crack one in well under a thousandth of a second. That’s very hard to beat.
But we don’t have one system. We have a thousand, each starting from its own random position and getting its own random shoves. At every step, we need a thousand fresh plans.
Here’s where the two approaches differ:

The one-at-a-time approach solves the thousand puzzles one after another, using a well-known solver called SCS. It’s a bit like a single brilliant runner delivering a thousand letters, one trip at a time.
The all-together approach uses Jaddle on a graphics card (GPU). All thousand chains have the same springs, motors and rules; only their positions differ. So Jaddle solves all thousand puzzles side by side, in lockstep, like a marching band where every musician takes the same step at the same time.

Both approaches use a warm start: each new plan begins from the previous step’s plan, shifted forward by one step. Since the world hasn’t changed much in half a second, the old plan is usually a great starting guess.

title: Herding a Thousand Springy Robots
text:
And the winner is…
It depends on how many systems you have, which is the most interesting part of the whole example.

One system: the one-at-a-time solver wins. A single tiny puzzle leaves a GPU almost entirely idle; it spends most of its time just getting started.
Tens of systems: the batched approach catches up.
A thousand systems: the batched approach on a laptop GPU spends about one-fortieth as long per puzzle as the one-at-a-time solver, and its plans are slightly more accurate too. Even running the batched approach on an ordinary CPU, it’s about three times faster than looping.
Ten thousand systems: something new happens…

title: Herding a Thousand Springy Robots
section: The slowest member of the band
text:
The slowest member of the band
Remember the marching band? The band only finishes when its slowest member finishes. In a fleet of ten thousand, there are always a few chains in a tricky spot, perhaps just shoved past the edge of their safe zone, and their puzzles take longer to solve. Everyone else ends up waiting for them.
The fix is something every real controller needs anyway: a deadline. We give the solver a fixed amount of effort per step. Any system that hasn’t fully finished by then simply uses the best plan it has so far. Because Jaddle always keeps its answers within the motor limits as it works, even an unfinished plan never asks a motor to do the impossible.
With a deadline in place, the time per puzzle for ten thousand systems drops back down near its best.

title: Herding a Thousand Springy Robots
text:
Do they agree?
Speed is no use if the answers are wrong. So we check both approaches against a reference answer solved to extremely high accuracy. Both are close, and over the whole run, the two fleets end up with nearly identical total costs. The blocks stay calm, the motors stay within their limits, and the chains settle down in both cases.

title: Herding a Thousand Springy Robots
text:
The takeaway
This example isn’t saying “always use a GPU”. If you’re controlling one robot and need an answer within a strict fraction of a millisecond, a traditional CPU solver is still the right tool.
But a surprising number of real problems involve lots of similar decisions at once: a fleet of delivery robots, a wind farm full of turbines, or testing one controller against thousands of possible futures to see how it copes. In those cases, it’s worth asking the marching-band question: could all of these take the same step together? When the answer is yes, solving them side by side can be dramatically faster than solving them one at a time.

title: Jaddle on the hard MIPLIB LP benchmark: 382 of 383
text:
With default settings, Jaddle certified 382 of the 383 LP relaxations in the PDLP papers’ hard MIPLIB 2017 set, to a relative tolerance of 1e-4, on a single laptop GPU. The shifted geometric mean solve time was 6.9 seconds, and half the instances finished in under 3.2 seconds.
Jaddle is a saddle-point solver written entirely in JAX, so it runs unchanged on CPU, GPU and TPU. Its algorithm is explained in the How Jaddle Works post. First-order LP solvers are fast per iteration but have a reputation for being fragile. Some instances stall for thousands of iterations, and the usual fix is per-instance tuning. This article shows that a fixed configuration can clear almost the whole benchmark.
It also looks at the one instance that did not converge, hgms62. It was within a factor of about four of the tolerance when the clock ran out. Changing one setting from its default gets it over the line.

title: Jaddle on the hard MIPLIB LP benchmark: 382 of 383
text:
The benchmark set
The test set is the 383 MIPLIB 2017 instances used to evaluate PDLP and cuPDLP, taken from the mip_relaxations_instance_list in FirstOrderLp.jl. Each instance has between 100,000 and 10 million nonzeros. Integrality is dropped, so every instance is solved as a plain LP.
The set is hard for first-order methods for reasons that have little to do with size:

Wide coefficient ranges. Many instances mix coefficients of 1 with big-M terms of 1e6 or more. Diagonal scaling cannot fully remove this, and it slows Jaddle down a lot.
Hidden objectives. Some models put the objective in a dense equality row, such as min z subject to z = Σ aⱼxⱼ. The real cost structure is then hidden in the constraints, and the primal iterates drift off feasibility.
Degeneracy and long tails. Many relaxations have large optimal faces or near-parallel constraints. Iterates then circle the optimum for a long time before the duality gap closes.

The instances range from 150 to 1.45 million columns and from 36 to 2.95 million rows. One configuration has to handle all of them.

An instance counts as converged when Jaddle returns a full optimality certificate on the presolved LP. All three residuals must be below the tolerance. Jaddle does not stop on a heuristic such as objective stalling.
The headline time is the iteration loop, including the one-off XLA compile on the first epoch. Wall time adds presolve, scaling, setup and postsolve. Unsolved instances count at the full 3,600 seconds in every average, as in the PDLP papers.

Why a tolerance of 1e-4
A relative tolerance of 1e-4 is the “quick and ready” setting. It puts the objective within about 0.01% of optimal, with constraint violations of the same relative size. For many uses that is the answer:

Planning and what-if runs, where the input data is far less accurate than 1e-4.
MIP root relaxations and bounds, where a near-optimal dual bound is what matters.
Warm starts and crossover. A 1e-4 point is close enough to the optimal face that a simplex repair is cheap. On mzzv11, crossover from a 1e-4 point took 125 to 6,077 pivots, against 47,774 for HiGHS’s simplex from a cold start.

First-order methods also slow down as they approach the optimum, so each extra digit costs more than the last. Stopping at 1e-4 keeps the solver where it is fastest. The PDLP papers use 1e-4 as their moderate-accuracy level, which makes the results comparable.
When more accuracy is needed, Jaddle provides tools that start from a 1e-4 solution: feasibility polishing (jl.solve_with_polishing), iterative refinement (jl.solve_with_refinement) and crossover to an exact vertex (jl.crossover).

title: Jaddle on the hard MIPLIB LP benchmark: 382 of 383
section: Presolve: HiGHS plus a Jaddle-specific reduction
text:
Presolve: HiGHS plus a Jaddle-specific reduction
Each instance goes through jl.solve_with_presolve with the defined-variable elimination switched on. It runs five steps:

HiGHS presolve removes redundant rows and columns, fixes variables and tightens bounds.
Defined-variable elimination, Jaddle’s own reduction, removes dense defining rows that HiGHS keeps.
Jaddle solves the reduced LP.
Elimination postsolve recovers the eliminated variables and the duals of their rows.
HiGHS postsolve maps the primal and dual solution back to the original model.

Presolve is cheap next to the solve. The median presolve time was 0.28 seconds. HiGHS kept a median of 95% of the columns. Presolve also solved one instance outright: neos-787933, with 236,376 columns, which counts as one of the 382.

Why Jaddle needs its own presolve
Standard presolvers are built for simplex and interior-point methods, which factorise matrices. For those methods, fill-in is expensive and a dense row is cheap. Jaddle has the opposite trade-off. It only does matrix-vector products, so extra nonzeros cost little. But some row structures damage the conditioning that decides how fast it converges.
The worst of these is a defined variable: a row a·z + r·x = b that defines z as a combination of other variables. In gmut-* and leo1, z is a zero-cost aggregate whose coefficients mirror the objective. In proteindesign*, z is the objective itself: min z subject to z = Σ aⱼxⱼ. In both cases, the dense row hides the objective structure from the scaling, and the primal iterates drift off feasibility.
HiGHS and SCIP leave these rows alone for three reasons. z is not a column singleton, because inequality rows use it too. It is not free, so substituting it needs an explicit bound row. And substituting a dense row breaks their fill-in limits.


What the elimination does
jaddle.presolve.eliminate_defined_variables substitutes z = E·x + const throughout the model:

The cost of z moves onto x, and any constant goes into the objective offset.
Inequality rows that use z get the substitution added to them.
Bounds on z become rows on x, unless the bounds on x already imply them.

The rules are conservative. A zero-cost aggregate row needs at least 100 nonzeros to qualify. An objective row qualifies from 2 nonzeros, because a short objective row hides the objective just as well. z may appear in at most four inequality rows. Total fill-in is capped at the original nonzero count. Later passes follow objective chains only, pushing the cost down onto the decision variables. On radiationm40-10-02, for example, min z, z = 1601 N + T is followed by rows that define N and T.
The postsolve recovers both the eliminated primal values and the duals of the removed rows. The mapped primal-dual pair is exactly as feasible and optimal as the reduced one.

title: Jaddle on the hard MIPLIB LP benchmark: 382 of 383
section: Case study: hgms62, the one that got away
text:
Case study: hgms62, the one that got away
hgms62 is the only instance Jaddle did not certify with default settings. It ran for the full hour, about 2.9 million iterations, and stopped close to the tolerance but not inside it.

The instance
hgms62 has 48,597 columns and 582,237 rows, or 37,235 by 569,830 after presolve. Size is not the problem. It ranks 46th by file size, and rwth-timetable, ten times larger, certified in 10 seconds. Its half-size sibling, hgms30, is telling. It was the second-slowest certified instance, taking 3,869 epochs and 1,190 seconds. The hgms family is hard for Jaddle because of its structure, and hgms62 is about twice the size of hgms30.
The family has a history in Jaddle’s development. On hgms30, an earlier version locked into a single restart cycle for more than 1,250 epochs, with the objective stuck 7% off optimal. That led to the artificial restart rule in the current solver, which forces a restart when a cycle runs too long without progress.


How close it got
When the clock ran out, the postsolved point had these residuals on the original LP:

The primal was feasible to tolerance. The dual feasibility and the gap were the problem: still converging, but slowly. A 600-second run of an earlier build had left them at 1.7e-2 and 8.5e-2, so the solver was making steady progress, not stalling. It just needed more time than the limit allowed.


The fix: widen the diagonal clamp
The default that matters here is diag_clamp. Jaddle starts from Ruiz and Pock–Chambolle scaling, then adapts a per-coordinate diagonal metric at each restart. Coordinates that drift steadily get larger steps, and coordinates that oscillate get smaller ones. This adaptive scaling is on by default, because it cut the shifted geometric mean solve time on this benchmark by about 18%.
diag_clamp limits how far that adaptation can move each coordinate from the baseline scaling. The default of 10 keeps every scale factor in [1/10, 10]. That is a safe bound across the whole benchmark, but on hgms62 it is too tight. The likely reason is that some coordinates need more rescaling than a factor of 10 allows, so the clamp holds them back.
Raising diag_clamp greatly lets the adaptive metric correct the scaling fully, and hgms62 then converges. Nothing else changes: the same presolve, tolerance and time limit.
import jaddle.jaddle_linear as jl

result = jl.solve_with_presolve(
    "hgms62.mps",
    eliminate_defined_vars=True,  # as in the benchmark
    primal_feasibility_tolerance=1e-4,
    dual_feasibility_tolerance=1e-4,
    dual_gap_tolerance=1e-4,
    diag_clamp=1e8,  # default 10.0
)
With this setting, hgms62 converges in 73.65 seconds.


Why the default stays at 10
A wider clamp is not a free win. The adaptive metric changes the geometry the solver works in, and a loose bound gives it more room to go wrong on other instances. Jaddle’s primal weight shows the same risk: with a wide k_scale clamp and per-epoch updates it ran away on mzzv11, reaching 1e8 with the gap stuck at 0.94. The default is set for the whole benchmark, not for its hardest member.
This is the pattern for a first-order solver: one robust default that handles 382 of 383 instances, and a small set of documented settings for the rare instance that needs more. When a solve stalls, diag_clamp is a good first setting to try. Turning adaptive scaling off with diag_adapt=False is another.

title: Jaddle on the hard MIPLIB LP benchmark: 382 of 383
text:
Caveats and reproducing the run
Three points matter when reading these numbers.

The certificate is on the presolved LP. After HiGHS postsolve, 297 of the 383 points also pass the 1e-4 certificate on the original LP. Postsolve can enlarge a first-order solution’s small dual errors. Presolve can also rescale a problem a lot, which changes what a relative tolerance means. On leo1, presolve folds a row with 1e7 coefficients into the cost, so the objective is right but the original dual test fails. When the original certificate matters, polishing, iterative refinement or crossover can tighten the postsolved point.
The time limit matters for the hardest few. With a 600-second limit, earlier runs certified 380 of 383. hgms30 and fhnw-binschedule1 need 20 to 26 minutes.
GPU runs are not bit-for-bit repeatable. The order of scatter-add operations varies, so identical runs can differ by several epochs.

The MPS files are not shipped with Jaddle. Download the 383 instances from the MIPLIB 2017 site into data/, then run from the repository root:
python benchmarks/benchmark.py --tol 1e-4 --max-seconds 3600 --highs-solver none
--highs-solver none skips the HiGHS reference solve, which can take longer than Jaddle’s. Add --diag-clamp 1e8 to rerun hgms62 with the wider clamp. The harness and its options are documented in benchmarks/README.md.

title: Max-Cut: The Art of Splitting a Room
text:
Imagine you’re organising a quiz night with 30 people, and you need to split them into two teams. There’s a complication: some pairs of people simply cannot stop bickering. You’ve drawn a map of every bickering pair. Your goal is to put as many of those pairs as possible on opposite teams, so they’re too busy competing to argue with each other.
This puzzle has a name, Max-Cut, and it is famously, stubbornly hard.

title: Max-Cut: The Art of Splitting a Room
text:
Drawing the problem
Mathematicians picture this as a graph: a set of dots (the people) joined by lines (the bickering pairs). Splitting the people into two teams is like drawing a line across the page. Every connection that crosses your line counts as “cut”, and you want to cut as many as possible.
In our example there are 30 people, and each pair has a 30% chance of being a bickering pair. That gives a graph with 119 connections.

title: Max-Cut: The Art of Splitting a Room
text:
Why it’s hard
With 30 people, each person can go on one of two teams, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 × … (thirty times) possible splits. That’s over a billion options. Add one more person and the number doubles. Add ten more and it’s a thousand times bigger.
Checking every option is hopeless for big graphs, and as far as anyone knows, there’s no clever shortcut that always finds the perfect answer quickly. Max-Cut belongs to a family of problems called NP-hard, which is computer-science speak for “nobody knows how to solve these fast, and many people suspect nobody ever will.”
So we settle for the next best thing: an answer that’s provably close to perfect.

title: Max-Cut: The Art of Splitting a Room
text:
The trick: pretend it’s easier
In 1995, Michel Goemans and David Williamson came up with a beautiful idea.
In the real problem, each person has to pick a team. You could picture each person holding a compass needle that must point either straight north (Team North) or straight south (Team South). Bickering pairs want their needles pointing in opposite directions.
Now let’s loosen the rules. Instead of only north or south, each person’s needle can point in any direction at all, not just on a flat map but in a space with many dimensions. Bickering pairs still want their needles to point as far apart as possible, but now there’s a whole sphere of in-between options.
This loosened version is called a relaxation, and it has two wonderful properties:

It’s much easier to solve. The relaxed problem is a type of puzzle called a semidefinite program, which, unlike the original, can be solved efficiently and exactly.
Its answer is a ceiling. Since every real split is also allowed in the relaxed version (north and south are still valid directions), the relaxed problem can only do better than or equal to the real one. So its score tells us: no split can possibly cut more than this.

title: Max-Cut: The Art of Splitting a Room
section: Back to reality: the random slice
text:
Back to reality: the random slice
Of course, people can’t actually join “Team Slightly North-East-Up”. We need to turn the needle directions back into two teams.
Goemans and Williamson’s answer is delightfully simple: slice the space with a random flat sheet. Everyone whose needle points to one side of the sheet goes on one team; everyone on the other side goes on the other.
Why does this work? Bickering pairs ended up with needles pointing far apart. The further apart two needles point, the more likely a random sheet will pass between them, putting them on opposite teams. Pairs who got along fine ended up with needles close together, so they’ll usually stay on the same side.






TipThe famous guarantee



Goemans and Williamson proved that, on average, a random slice cuts at least 87.8% as many connections as the ceiling. Since the ceiling is at least as good as the best possible split, the slice is guaranteed to be close to optimal, without ever finding the optimum.


That was a landmark result. For decades, nobody has found an efficient method with a better guarantee, and there are good theoretical reasons to believe nobody can.
In our example, we try 100 random slices and keep the best one. It comfortably clears the 87.8% bar.

title: Max-Cut: The Art of Splitting a Room
text:
A certificate of quality
There’s one more neat feature. When the solver finishes the relaxed problem, it also produces a set of numbers, one per person, called dual values. Add them all up and you get exactly the same ceiling, approached from the opposite direction.
This acts like a certificate. Anyone can take those numbers and check, without re-solving anything, that no split could ever beat the ceiling. You don’t have to trust the solver; you can verify its homework.

title: Max-Cut: The Art of Splitting a Room
text:
How Jaddle solves it
The tricky bit of the relaxed problem is a rule saying the needle directions must “fit together” consistently. (In technical terms, a certain table of numbers must be positive semidefinite.) Jaddle handles this by taking small steps towards a better answer and, after each step, nudging the result back into the set of answers that fit together.
The example writes the problem in CVXPY, a popular language for describing optimisation problems, and hands it to Jaddle to solve. We double-check Jaddle’s ceiling against SCS, another well-established solver, and they agree.

title: Max-Cut: The Art of Splitting a Room
Small Problems? Use Clarabel. Big Problems? Use Jaddle.
text:
Imagine you need to get across town. You could take one expensive sports car that makes the trip in a few careful, powerful moves. Or you could take a bus that makes lots of small, cheap stops, one after another. For one passenger, the sports car wins. For a thousand passengers, the bus is the only sensible choice.
Optimisation solvers face the same choice. Some solvers make a small number of very careful, expensive steps. Others make many quick, cheap steps. Which one wins depends on the size of the problem, and it’s a lesson I keep running into across my recent posts.

title: Small Problems? Use Clarabel. Big Problems? Use Jaddle.
section: Two ways to climb a hill
text:
Two ways to climb a hill
Finding the best answer to an optimisation problem is a bit like climbing a hill in thick fog. You can’t see the top, but you can feel which way is uphill, and you keep moving that way.
Some solvers, such as Clarabel, take careful steps. Each step is expensive: the solver works out a lot about the shape of the hill around it, which means solving a sizeable calculation. Because each step is so well-informed, you need only a few of them to reach the top.
Jaddle takes a different approach. Its steps are cheap. Each one is a handful of quick sums, the sort of arithmetic a computer can repeat at great speed. You need many more steps to reach the top, but each one costs very little.

title: Small Problems? Use Clarabel. Big Problems? Use Jaddle.
section: Why many cheap steps can win
text:
Why many cheap steps can win
It sounds backwards. Surely a few smart steps should beat lots of dumb ones? Not always. Here’s the catch: the cost of one careful step grows quickly as the problem gets bigger. Double the size of the problem and a careful step can cost several times as much. A cheap step grows much more gently. Eventually the careful solver spends so long on each step that the cheap solver, taking far more steps, still arrives first.
There’s a second benefit too. Cheap steps are easy to run in parallel. A graphics card, for example, is built to do thousands of simple sums at the same time. Lots of small, similar steps fit that kind of hardware beautifully.

title: Small Problems? Use Clarabel. Big Problems? Use Jaddle.
text:
The evidence
I’ve tried this on several problems in the series, and the picture is consistent.
Small problems: the careful solver wins. When I ran a robust Kalman filter, which tracks a moving object through noisy and sometimes wrong measurements, Clarabel finished in a fraction of a second. Jaddle took a few seconds. On a 30-node version of the network-splitting puzzle, the same story held: SCS was far quicker. The problems were small enough that the cheap steps didn’t have enough work to add up.
Big problems: the cheap solver wins. On a network with 1,000 nodes and about 150,000 links, which means a grid of a million numbers to arrange, SCS took about 126 seconds. Jaddle finished in about 18 seconds, roughly seven times faster, and both reached the same answer.
Many problems at once: the cheap solver wins. When I controlled a fleet of 1,000 small machines, each one needed its own plan every moment. Solving them one at a time with SCS took about 420 microseconds per plan. Jaddle, solving all the plans together in one batch, took about 10 microseconds each, around forty times faster on a laptop graphics card. Even on an ordinary processor, the batched version was about three times faster than the one-at-a-time approach.

title: Small Problems? Use Clarabel. Big Problems? Use Jaddle.
text:
The honest bit
This is not a magic trick, and the crossover is real. On a single small problem, the careful solver is usually the right choice, and I’d rather tell you that than sell you something you don’t need. Jaddle’s advantage shows up when problems are large, or when you have many of them to solve together. If you’re solving one tiny problem a week, use the specialist tool.

title: Small Problems? Use Clarabel. Big Problems? Use Jaddle.
text:
A quick decision guide

One small problem, needed occasionally: use Clarabel.
One large problem: try Jaddle, and compare it against Clarabel on your own data.
Many similar problems at once: Jaddle, especially batched on a GPU.
You need a high-accuracy answer fast on a tiny problem: Clarabel. Its careful steps pay off when precision matters more than throughput.

title: Small Problems? Use Clarabel. Big Problems? Use Jaddle.
text:
The takeaway
When you choose a solver, don’t ask only which one is cleverest. Ask how big your problem is, how many you need to solve, and whether a crowd of cheap steps can beat a small team of expensive ones. For small problems, use Clarabel. For big ones, lots of cheap steps often win, and Jaddle is built around exactly that idea.
